title: Oz national debt passes $1 trillion
full_text:
Australia’s governments will have a combined $2 trillion in debt by the end of the decade, putting the country at risk if it is hit by another significant economic shock.
Federal government debt ticked over $1 trillion on Thursday, on the same day new data showed national unemployment had ticked up more than expected in July to reach 4.5 per cent.
Markets and some economists believe it will mean interest rates are held steady when the Reserve Bank next meets at the end of September.
But Labor has been accused of stoking inflation and putting Australians at risk of more interest rate rises by putting public spending on the nations’ credit cards.
“Today’s debt is tomorrow’s taxes and the debt the Albanese government is racking up is being spent as fuel for inflation, making the damage so much greater”, shadow treasurer Tim Wilson said.
Treasurer Jim Chalmers said the country would have reached the grim debt milestone years earlier if the Coalition was still in power.
“If the Coalition had been in power today, gross debt this year would already be approaching $1.2 trillion,” Dr Chalmers said. “The government’s responsible economic management has got debt down from what we inherited from the Coalition, and Australia is avoiding more than $70 billion in interest.” Independent economist Saul Eslake said although the figure was eye-watering, Australia’s debt-to-GDP ratio of 33 per cent was much lower than the UK, Japan, Germany and the US – which on Thursday hit $40 trillion in debt.
“But that’s not to say it’s good, and one of the fastest growing areas of spending for the federal government and every state except (WA) is interest,” he said.
“And the fact that every government except WA is continuing to run big deficits means they’re increasingly exposed to the risk of higher interest rates globally … If you’re not running cash surpluses, you can’t stop adding to debt.” Mr Eslake said that the more states’ revenues were eaten up by interest, the more at risk they were if and when there was another economic shock.
According to the Parliamentary Budget Office analysis which found combined debt would reach $2trn by 2030, the interest costs of paying off debt will also grow to take up a larger share of government revenue.
For Queensland – which has identified ballooning infrastructure costs as a key risk – it will grow from 2.8 per cent in 2024-25 to 6.8 per cent by 2029-30.
Meanwhile, Australia’s unemployment rate ticked up to 4.5 per cent in July, a higher rate than expected.
Employment Minister Amanda Rishworth said the Treasury and the Reserve Bank expected some softening in the labour market, but the rate was still a “historically very low number”.
Betashares chief economist David Bassanese said the RBA would likely view the July result as “finally bringing the labour market into better balance”. “Along with slowing house prices, and the recent lower-than-expected June quarter inflation result, it’s another reason to expect the RBA to remain benched at the upcoming late-September policy meeting,” he said, adding that July inflation data, out next week, could change things.
